LOCAL GOVERNMENT ELECTORAL REGISTRATION SYSTEM 
 
The LGERS project is an initiative led by the Department of Housing, Local Government and 
Heritage to create a centralised, modernised electoral registration system for Ireland.  
  
Ireland’s electoral registers have historically been maintained separately by each local 
authority, leading to inconsistencies and inaccuracies.   Voter.ie will become the new 
national registration system and is due to come into effect by the end of 2026 replacing the 
current checktheregister.ie.  
OBJECTIVE 
The project aims to improve the accuracy, accessibility, and efficiency of Ireland’s electoral 
register, addressing longstanding issues such as duplicate entries, redundant records (e.g., 
deceased individuals or electors who have moved away), and fragmented data management 
across local authorities ensuring a more reliable foundation for democratic processes. 
LEGAL FRAMEWORK 
The project aligns with the Electoral Reform Act 2022, which provides the legal basis for 
modernising the electoral process, including voter registration.  
KEY FEATURES  
• Centralised System - LGERS will transition local authorities to a shared national 
electoral registration system by the end of 2026, replacing separate local databases. 
This will streamline voter registration and updates. 
• Identity Verification - A significant feature is the use of Personal Public Service 
Numbers (PPSNs) to verify voter identities.  
• Accessibility  - The LGERS system will build on the checktheregister.ie platform, 
allowing voters to register or update details online easily.

6 
 
• Data Integrity - LGERS enables cross-checking with the Department of Social 
Protection to confirm identity details (name, date of birth, PPSN), ensuring the 
register’s accuracy while protecting sensitive data like PPSNs from public disclosure. 
FUNDING AND RESOURCES 
In 2025, the government allocated over €3 million to local authorities for LGERS, including 
€1.7 million for data quality improvements and funding for two additional staff members 
per local authority to address data issues before the 2026 transition. 
  
The Electoral Commission’s first “Oversight Report on Electoral Registers” in May 2025 
noted that while LGERS will help centralise and streamline the registration process, it alone 
will not fully resolve legacy accuracy issues. Additional work is required to address data gaps 
and discrepancies between local authority registers.  
  
Galway County Council’s franchise team have intensified data cleanup efforts in recent 
weeks to remove duplicates, verify identities and prepare for the transition to a national 
system.  
THE FOLLOWING WORK IS CURRENTLY ONGOING IN THE REGISTER OF ELECTORS 
• 1,500 letters have issued to potential duplicate electors in recent weeks  
• Deaths recorded by the General Register Office are cross referenced against 
electoral register on a weekly basis to ensure deceased electors details are removed 
from the register.    
• Preparing data from polling cards returned during the 2024 electoral events to 
identify and remove redundant entries from the register.   
• All townland names (5,000 approx.) are being translated in advance of the transition 
to LGERS in line with the Official Languages (Amendment) Act 2021 and an Scéim 
Teanga.  
  
Galway County Council are currently on track to have LGERS fully implemented by the end 
of 2026.

WATER SAFETY AND LIFEGUARD SERVICES – SUMMER 2025 UPDATE 
  
County Galway boasts a stunning and diverse coastline that continues to attract water 
enthusiasts throughout the summer months. As schools break for the holidays and visitor 
numbers increase, ensuring a safe and enjoyable aquatic environment is a top priority. 
  
With the bathing season now underway, Galway County Council is committed to promoting 
water safety and providing high-quality supervision at designated bathing areas. The Council 
employs a full-time Water Safety Awareness and Development Officer who oversees the 
management of bathing areas and coordinates the delivery of the seasonal lifeguard service 
across both Galway County and City. 
Lifeguard services have officially commenced in line with the Summer Ready Plan 2025. 
Lifeguards are now on duty at 16 designated beaches. It is important to note that no flag 
displayed means no lifeguard is on duty.

COOP4RURALGOV, COOPERATION FOR RURAL GOVERNANCE RURAL PROOFING 
Cooperation for better sparsely populated rural, coastal and mountain focused 
governance. 
On June 17–18, 2025, Galway County Council welcomed partners from Spain, Ireland, 
Estonia, and Bulgaria for an interregional workshop on the topic “Building on the steps 
required to Embed Rural Proofing at Local, Regional and National Level.  
The workshop focused on embedding Rural Proofing in policy design and delivery at local, 
regional, and national levels.

The workshop brought together policymakers, technical experts, and rural development 
practitioners to test and refine a practical impact assessment tool designed specifically to 
make rural sensitivities visible in policy planning. The first day began with an overview of the 
assessment process led by Maria Hall (Hub Planning). 
The goal: to ensure that rural voices and realities are considered from the earliest stages of 
decision-making. The workshop provided a valuable opportunity to assess whether this 
approach is clear, usable, and practical—and whether it can help policymakers identify risks 
and opportunities early, especially those unique to rural settings. 
Rural communities face distinct challenges, but those challenges are often overlooked in 
policy planning. This workshop aimed to build a stronger foundation for evidence-informed, 
people centred policy design by piloting an impact assessment tool and examined a 
Structured, Hands-On Methodology which was Presented by Maria Hall, Hub Planning 
utilising existing Data and Consultation feedback and utilisation of Artificial Intelligence Bot.  
This process was 
designed to test 
and refine a 
practical method 
for assessing the 
potential impacts 
of rural policy 
projects on people 
and places. By 
applying an Impact 
Assessment Matrix 
to a case study policy scenario, (Case Study to test the impact of closure of Post Offices in 
Rural Areas) participants explored how structured evaluation tools can support better rural-
proofed decision-making. 
WHAT WE DID 
Over two days, participants worked in small groups, applying a step-by-step method: 
• Scoping Potential Impacts: Identifying possible social, environmental, and economic 
effects of a policy scenario. 
• Deepening Understanding: 
Using data and consultation 
findings to understand who 
might be affected and how. 
• Assessing Significance: Rating 
the scale, duration, severity, 
and likelihood of impacts using 
a clear, structured matrix.

16 
 
• Developing Mitigation Strategies: Identifying practical measures to reduce negative 
impacts and enhance benefits. 
KEY LESSONS 
• Structured Does Not Mean Rigid: Using clear steps and rating tables allowed 
participants to focus on real impacts while maintaining flexibility to discuss what 
matters most for rural areas. 
• Data and Local Knowledge Are Equally Important: The process highlighted the power 
of combining statistical data with lived experience and consultation insights. 
• Data and Local Knowledge Are Equally Important: The process highlighted the power 
of combining statistical data with lived experience and consultation insights. 
• Actionable Outcomes: The matrix helped groups move from identifying impacts to 
concrete mitigation and enhancement measures, ensuring that discussions 
translated into practical next steps. 
• Early Assessment Helps Avoid Later Problems: Testing impacts at the design stage, 
rather than after decisions are made, can help prevent negative consequences for 
rural communities. 
WHY THIS MATTERS 
Rural proofing is not just a policy aspiration; it requires methods that are clear, usable, and 
useful for governments, local authorities, and communities. The workshop in Ireland 
showed that a structured Impact Assessment approach can: 
 
 Identify rural-specific sensitivities early 
 
 Guide practical mitigation strategies 
 
 Build confidence in rural-proofed decision-making 
 
 Ensure people-centred policies 
A Structured, Hands-On Methodology 
Our two-day workshop in Ireland piloted an Impact Assessment Matrix to see whether 
structured tools could help surface these 
issues early and guide practical mitigation 
strategies. 
The group brainstormed practical 
responses: what can be done to minimise 
harm, enhance positives, or make 
adjustments that reduce community risk? 
Identifying any positive or negative social impacts that are likely to result from the 
development application with respect (examples could include):

17 
 
Community values - potential implications to cultural and community wellbeing as a result of 
the project including impacts on residents and surrounding properties, social exclusion, social 
cohesion, community safety and health. 
Safety and amenity - analysis of potential adverse impacts on local amenity (both short and 
longer term) including noise, air quality and visual impacts, with particular focus on the how 
the demolition/transition phase of the development would be managed.  
Aged care demand - actual or projected population growth within the catchment and aged 
care demand  
Access and connectivity – presence or absence of safe and accessible public transport for 
patrons, availability of car parking and time restrictions on car parking (if any)  
Community facilities – identify if the increased demand for supports and services.  
Demand on services – such as public transport, convenience food, medical centres and 
community services and identify if the communal facilities would have the capacity to service 
residents during the transition stages of the development.  
Suitability of type, mix and capacity – nature and extent suitability. 
PRESENTATION BY MARIA HALL, HUB PLANNING 
Insights from Ireland: Participation and Policy in Practice 
Provided a deep dive into the Irish experience with Public Participation Networks (PPNs). 
Maria Hall presented findings from a recent review of PPNs, which serve as formal platforms 
for civil society to engage with local authorities. Discussions explored their effectiveness in 
representing diverse groups—such as older persons, people with disabilities, and members 
of the Traveller community—and their role in shaping inclusive policy. 
Later in the day, Sinéad Quinn, from Ireland’s Department of Rural and Community 
Development, shared the national approach to Rural Proofing as outlined in the 
strategy Our Rural Future. Her presentation illustrated how over 150 cross-government 
commitments are being mobilized to foster economic diversification, reverse rural decline, 
and strengthen rural resilience. 
Presentation by Sinead Quinn, Rural Strategy Unit, Department of rural and Community 
Development and the Gaeltacht outlined the following.

Ireland 
• Government Decision in 1999 
• Government Handbook amended 
• Requires Memo for Government to 
indicate the impact on rural communities 
• Rural referred to ‘towns and villages and in smaller urban centres outside of the five

NEW APPROACH TO RURAL PROOFING 
Government commitment: Our Rural Future 2021-2025 (Measure 148) to develop “an 
effective rural proofing model to ensure that the needs of rural communities are considered 
in the development of Government policies”  
DRCDG commissioned research, including looking at the international experience, and 
developments by OECD and EU. 
KEY LEARNINGS:   
• Rural proofing has been difficult to successfully develop  
• No ‘one size fits all’ approach  
PILOT ON RURAL PROOFING: 
 
• Pilot exercise to apply rural proofing concepts to four key initiatives 
• Led to an understanding that Rural Proofing is not a policy or a model  
• Rural Proofing is a process to view policy development through a rural lens 
• To help ensure government policies and services understand and take account of 
specific needs and capacity of rural communities 
PILOT LEARNINGS: 
• Early consideration to identify issues and capacities of rural areas 
• Public consultations should systematically prompt rural communities to reflect and 
advise on policies/proposals  
• Place-based approach to rural development can enable meaningful engagement 
with rural people and business 
• Policy makers should be supported by guidance material to undertake Rural Proofing 
 
GUIDE TO RURAL PROOFING FOR POLICY MAKERS: 
• Pilot showed that a level of Rural Proofing is being undertaken within the current 
system, although not always expressed as Rural Proofing 
• Any new approach needed to be practical and implementable 
• Objective was to build on and strengthen those approaches  
 
Developed a “Guide to Rural Proofing for Policy Makers”

Core aim is to clearly and simply explain what rural proofing is, what is meant by rural, and 
provide guidance and assistance.

RURAL PACT – WHAT IS IT 
A framework for cooperation between public authorities, civil society, businesses, academia 
and citizens, at the European, national, regional and local level; the aim of which is mobilize 
stakeholders to act on the needs and aspirations of rural communities by 2040 (European 
Union, n. da). Rural Pact was launched by the European Commission in 2021 as part of the 
Long-Term Vision for the EU’s rural areas (European Commission, 2021b). 
DIALOGUE, COORDINATION, AND NEXT STEPS 
Day two of the workshop focused on refining the assessment results and reflecting 
collectively on the process. A partner Steering Committee meeting closed the session, 
offering space to consolidate learning and discuss next steps for integrating this 
methodology into real policy settings across regions. 
By bringing together diverse experiences from Spain, Ireland, Estonia, and Bulgaria, the 
Galway workshop reaffirmed the power of collaboration in advancing rural-sensitive 
governance. More than a technical exercise, it marked a step forward in building policies 
that not only reach rural areas—but are rooted in their voices, knowledge, and needs. 
Next Steps:  Review Comparative Study, which incorporates feedback from Partner Countries 
through Questionnaires completed in April and Focus groups interviews held in May 2025.

Galway County Council, with LAWPRO (Local Authority Waters Programme) and four other

POLLINATOR ZONES 
Purpose: These zones are established to provide habitats for pollinators such as bees, 
butterflies, and other insects. Pollinators are crucial for the reproduction of many plants and 
the overall health of ecosystems.

Implementation: The zones include a variety of native flowering plants that bloom at 
different times of the year, ensuring a continuous food supply for pollinators. These plants 
are carefully selected to thrive in the local climate and soil conditions. 
BIODIVERSITY INFORMATION BOARDS: 
Educational Outreach: Information boards have been installed, such as the one by the River 
Nanny near the swimming pool. These boards educate visitors about the importance of 
biodiversity and the specific species found in the area. 
COMMUNITY EMPLOYMENT SCHEME: 
Local community employment scheme is actively involved in maintaining and monitoring 
these biodiversity zones. This includes planting, weeding, and conducting biodiversity 
surveys. 
INTEGRATION WITH HERITAGE PLANS: 
Holistic Approach: The biodiversity initiatives are part of a broader Heritage and Biodiversity 
Plan launched by Galway County Council. This plan integrates biodiversity with cultural and 
built heritage, ensuring a comprehensive approach to conservation. 
SUSTAINABLE PRACTICES: 
Eco-friendly Maintenance: The maintenance of these zones follows sustainable practices, 
such as reducing the use of pesticides and promoting organic gardening techniques. This 
helps create a healthier environment for both wildlife and people. 
IMPACT AND FUTURE PLANS: 
Ecological Health: The creation of pollinator zones and other biodiversity initiatives 
contribute to the ecological health of the Palace Grounds. They help increase the population 
of pollinators, which in turn supports the growth of various plant species. 
These efforts in the Palace Grounds are a testament to Tuam's commitment to preserving 
and enhancing its natural heritage, ensuring that future generations can enjoy and benefit 
from a rich and diverse ecosystem.
